query: For Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state, the factors governing its phase stability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure are not understood well enough to account for the range of phases that may appear. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain this behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations relative to that baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: The emergence of a range of phases in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 during cooling from a high‐temperature BCC state is driven by a feedback loop between local compositional fluctuations and kinetic limitations. Under controlled slower cooling, local heterogeneities provide preferential nucleation sites that promote the formation of a metastable phase (e.g., FCC) in addition to the BCC matrix, whereas rapid quenching suppresses this transformation.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy stabilized in a high-temperature BCC state.
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of cooling rates and controlled thermal exposures (including isothermal holds in the 1250–1350 °C range) to allow or inhibit local atomic diffusion and compositional fluctuations.
generation.conditions: This hypothesis applies under thermal regimes where atomic mobility permits local reordering (i.e., slower cooling or controlled isothermal exposure) and does not apply when extreme rapid quenching suppresses diffusion.
generation.structural_mediator: Local compositional fluctuations and heterogeneities (such as at grain boundaries or within grains) that act as nucleation sites for secondary phases.
generation.mechanism: During slower cooling, increased residence time near a critical temperature range allows limited atomic diffusion so that local concentration variations can drive heterogeneous nucleation. These regions become feedback centers that lower the kinetic barrier for the emergence of a metastable phase (e.g., FCC), diverging from the uniform BCC structure observed in rapid quenched samples.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples cooled under conditions allowing sufficient diffusion (i.e., slower cooling or isothermal holds) will display a measurable increase in non-BCC phase fractions (e.g., FCC) compared to samples subjected to rapid quenching, which should remain predominantly BCC.
generation.baseline: Rapid quench conditions that preserve the high-temperature BCC state with minimal atomic diffusion and local compositional variations.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold only in processing windows where diffusion is neither completely suppressed (extreme rapid cooling) nor entirely equilibration-driven (very slow cools or extended annealing at high temperatures leading to equilibrium phases). In regimes outside these bounds, the transformation behavior may be governed by equilibrium thermodynamics rather than kinetic feedback.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the phase fraction change and the spatial distribution of the secondary phases remain uncertain due to the complex interplay between thermal gradients, diffusion rates, and local composition, requiring further quantitative analysis.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy samples: one set subjected to rapid quenching immediately from the high-temperature BCC state (baseline) and another set subjected to controlled slower cooling with an extended hold in the 1250–1350 °C range. Characterize the microstructure of both sets using EBSD, TEM, and XRD to quantify phase fractions and spatial distribution of phases.
measurements: Phase identification and quantification (BCC vs. FCC or other metastable phases) using XRD and EBSD.
Local compositional mapping via TEM/EDS to detect heterogeneities.
Grain morphology analysis to correlate microstructural features with cooling profiles.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the controlled slower cooling samples do not show a statistically significant increase in the formation of a secondary phase (e.g., FCC) or any measurable differences in local compositional segregation compared to the rapid quench baseline.

Results from developing such a material system (addition of Hf to the W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA) manufactured via magnetron-sputtering deposition with nanocrystalline grains are discussed. Computational thermodynamics approaches such as the CALPHAD method and density-functional theory-informed CE formalisms are used to select optimal compositions and predict thermodynamic properties. These compositions are then manufactured experimentally to test both their ion irradiation and hardness responses, aiming at validating modeling predictions. In this study, the microstructural evolution and thermal behavior of a Fe32Cr33Ni29Al3Ti3 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) fabricated by selective laser melting (SLM) were systematically investigated through a combination of experimental characterization and numerical simulation. The key conclusions are as follows: (1) Microstructural Variation: EBSD analysis revealed that increasing the laser power from 160 W to 200 W resulted in a higher fraction of the BCC phase (from 15% to 30%) and smaller FCC grain sizes. The BCC phase was primarily located in the upper melt pool regions, while nearly absent at the bottom. (2) Thermal Field Simulation: A 3D transient temperature field model incorporating a double-ellipsoid heat source and temperature-dependent properties accurately captured the thermal profiles during SLM. The elliptical melt pool shape and thermal gradients predicted by the model were consistent with experimental observations. (3) Melt Pool and Phase Formation: Residence time analysis showed that the bottom regions of the melt pool experienced shorter durations in the critical 1350–1250 °C range, limiting BCC nucleation. More recently, long-term annealing experiments at intermediate temperatures revealed that different crystalline phases could precipitate out of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA fcc matrix. Moreover, finite-temperature ab initio simulation results suggest that the free energy of the hcp (hexagonal-close-packing) crystallographic lattice in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA may be lowest at room temperature, compared with that of its bcc (body-centerd-cubic) and fcc counterparts. All these results cast doubt on the high structural stability of HEA lattices, which is obviously a critical and vital problem for our understanding and applications of these newly developed metallic materials and multicomponent oxides. However, until now the predicted hcp phase of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA has not been observed in any experiments and the question of viable polymorphism remains unanswered.
